Inverting the walking morphism

The geometric realization of \([1]\) is contractible. The checked proof identifies the functors out of \([1]\) that invert every arrow by evaluating their inversion data at the identity functor \([1]\to [1]\). This is an alternative to the manuscript’s argument enumerating the three arrows of \([1]\).

Use the Chapter 1 structures, walking-morphism and endpoint data, the Segal and commutative-square axioms, and Rezk. For a category \(D\), write \[ V_D=\Map ^{\Map ([1],[1])}([1],D),\qquad u\colon V_D\hookrightarrow \Map ([1],D). \] Thus \(V_D\) consists of functors inverting all arrows of \([1]\). Let \(c\colon D^\simeq \to \Map ([1],D)\) be the constant-arrow functor.

Supplementary Lemma 1. There is a functor \(k\colon D^\simeq \to V_D\) with \(uk=c\).

Proof idea

Constant arrows factor through the terminal category. That category is a groupoid, and a functor out of a groupoid inverts every arrow. Apply this to the universal family of objects of \(D\), then restrict the inverting family along \([1]\to \star \). The restriction computation identifies its underlying family with \(c\). □

Supplementary Lemma 2. There is a functor \(o\colon V_D\to D^\simeq \) with \(co=u\). The functor \(k\) of Supplementary Lemma 1 is an equivalence with inverse \(o\).

Proof idea

The defining pullback of \(V_D\) supplies a family of isomorphisms indexed by the arrows of \([1]\). Evaluate this family at the point of \(\Map ([1],[1])\) naming the identity functor. Its underlying arrow is the original functor \([1]\to D\): this is the identity computation for the mapping action, with the naming comparisons included.

Rezk identifies the anima of isomorphisms in \(D\) with \(D^\simeq \), by sending an object to its identity. Lifting the evaluated family through this equivalence gives \(o\) and the comparison \(co=u\). Both \(u\) and \(c\) are embeddings; for \(c\) this follows from Rezk and the embedding of isomorphisms among all arrows. The equations \(uk=c\) and \(co=u\) therefore imply \(ok=\operatorname {id}\) and \(ko=\operatorname {id}\) by reflection. These are identifications, not strict equalities of the chosen functors. □

Supplementary Corollary 3. In the setting of the localization definition, let \(l\colon [1]\to T\) be a localization at all arrows of \([1]\). Then \(T\) is contractible.

Proof idea

For every \(D\), the localization property gives an equivalence \(\rho _D\colon \Map (T,D)\iso V_D\). The composite of restriction along \(T\to \star \) with \(\rho _D\) is identified with \(k\). To check this comparison, compose with the embedding \(u\): both routes become the constant-arrow family, using the unit and composition comparisons for restriction and the terminal comparison \((T\to \star )l=([1]\to \star )\). Reflect through \(u\).

Since \(k\) and \(\rho _D\) are equivalences, restriction along \(T\to \star \) is an equivalence for every \(D\). Detection by mapping animae shows that \(T\to \star \) is an equivalence. No assumption that \(T\) is already a groupoid is used. □
